model.comments: High effort Claude Fable 5.1. Thinking is always on for Fable; depth is controlled by Anthropic's output_config.effort, which OpenRouter sets from reasoning.effort (its verbosity field maps to the same native field, so this equals the older opus-4.x verbosity convention).

prompt: # Role - You are an AI competing in a gaming arena. # Objective - Write a complete Python file that provides the next move for a Havannah on a 15x15 board. - You must define a smart policy that is able to beat other policies in the arena. - You will be disqualified if you do not return a legal move string. Therefore, you must always return a legal move string. # Required API The provided python file must implement the following API: ```python def policy(me: list[tuple[int, int]], opp: list[tuple[int, int]], valid_mask) -> tuple[int, int]: ... ``` # State Representation - You are always the player to move. - `me` is a list of (row, col) tuples for player-0 stones. - `opp` is a list of (row, col) tuples for player-1 stones. - `valid_mask` is a 2D array (shape NxN) where True marks playable cells on the Havannah board. - Rows and columns are 0-indexed in `0..14`, matching `valid_mask` indices. - A player wins when they complete one of three different structures from unbroken lines, or paths, of connected stones, all of their colour:- A ring is a loop around one or more cells (no matter whether the encircled cells are occupied by any player or empty[3]) - - A bridge, which connects any two of the six corner cells of the board - - A fork, which connects any three edges of the board; corner points are not considered parts of an edge - Note that the board is represented as a 2D array however internally it is a hexagonal grid. This requires extra spatial reasoning to determine the winning structures.Every stone not on the edge of the board is touching exactly 6 other stones (since they are hexagonal). - Two of those 6 stones are in the same column, two are in the left column, and two are in the right column. - Example: The store located at (4, 1) [i.e. b5] is touching b6 (5, 1) and b4 (3, 1) - and to its left is touching a4 (3, 0) and a5 (4, 0) - and to its right is touching c5 (4, 2) and c4 (3, 2) # Action / Return Format - Return a single move as a tuple `(row, col)`. - The chosen coordinate must satisfy `valid_mask[row][col] == True` and be unoccupied. - There is no pass move; always place a stone. # Constraints - You may use any standard Python imports, including numpy. - Your code is allowed 1 second of execution time on a modern 3GHz CPU. # Output Format Requirements - Output your strategy before providing the Python source code for your policy. - Output the Python source code for your policy surrounded by `...` tags. # Example Output The strategy for this policy is... ...
reasoning:
I'm figuring out the Havannah board geometry from the 15x15 array — a side-8 hex board has 169 cells matching that bounding box, so I need to work out how the adjacency structure maps onto it.

Testing the neighbor pattern around (4,1): it maps to (3,0), (4,0), (4,2), (3,2) plus (3,1) and (5,1), which is asymmetric for a standard axial system, so this looks like an offset "odd-q" style layout where odd columns shift, and column 1 being odd fits that pattern.

Working through the offset logic: if column 1 is shifted up half a row relative to columns 0 and 2, then cell (4,1) sits between rows 3 and 4 of the neighboring columns, explaining why both (3,0)/(4,0) and (3,2)/(4,2) are neighbors — so even columns are effectively shifted down relative to odd ones.

But I'm not confident this offset guess matches the actual board encoding. Since the valid_mask defines the true shape, I should instead figure out the coordinate system directly — likely axial coordinates for a hex board of size 8 embedded in a 15x15 grid, where validity is defined by constraints like |r-7|, |c-7|, and |(r-7)-(c-7)| all being at most 7.

Checking the given example, (4,1) is labeled "b5", meaning columns are letters and rows are 1-indexed. Tracing b5's neighbors against a4 and a5 tells me odd columns (like b) must be shifted upward relative to even columns for those adjacencies to hold.

Working out the full hexagon from this: column 7 (odd, center) spans 15 rows (0-14), while adjacent even columns 6 and 8 are shifted down and span 14 rows each (0-13). Continuing outward, column 5 covers rows 1-13 (13 cells), column 4 covers rows 1-12 (12 cells), column 3 covers rows 2-12 (11 cells), and I'm working out column 2's range next.

I realize I don't need to guess the exact offset direction -- I can just compute this from the valid_mask at runtime by checking which cells are actually valid, then deducing whether the layout follows an axial rhombus pattern (where row 0 has columns 7-14, row 7 has all 15, row 14 has columns 0-7) versus this offset hexagon pattern. The two shapes produce distinguishable column extents, so I can tell them apart programmatically.

I'll test several candidate neighbor systems—axial variants and offset variants—checking which produces exactly 6 corner cells with degree 3, 36 edge cells with degree 4, and 127 interior cells with degree 6, falling back to the example's convention if none match perfectly. Once I've identified corners, I'll find edges by removing corner cells from the boundary and grouping the remaining boundary cells into connected paths, since the boundary cycle should split into exactly 6 such edge segments between corners.

For win detection, I'm now thinking through how to track, for each connected group of stones, which corners and edges it touches using bitmasks—forming a bridge if it touches at least 2 corners, a fork if it touches at least 3 edges. The tricky part is detecting a ring, which requires checking whether the group encircles at least one cell, meaning some region of the complement is disconnected from the board's outer boundary.

A cleaner way to detect this: flood-fill the complement of the group from a virtual outside node, and any unreached cell signals a ring around empty or opponent stones; for the case where a group encircles its own stone, I need a separate check for a stone whose six neighbors are all part of the group.

A cell with all 6 neighbors in G is also encircled since those neighbors form a cycle around it, and boundary non-G cells always reach the outside so they're never falsely trapped. With ring detection settled via hex-adjacency flood fill, I'm moving on to think about the policy's time budget.

For a base-8 Havannah bot with a 1-second budget, a practical approach is: play a winning move immediately if available, block an immediate opponent win otherwise, and fall back on heuristics for everything else. Those heuristics would weigh connectivity toward edges/corners using shortest-path distances where empty cells cost 1 and own stones cost 0, plus fork potential across multiple targets.

I'm weighing this against MCTS with random playouts, but win-detection overhead per playout in Python likely limits me to only a few hundred simulations per second, so a well-tuned heuristic seems more reliable for outperforming similarly simple opponents.

I'm planning the heuristic to include win-in-1 and block-in-1 detection, plus checking for double threats, and sketching out the data structures needed: cell indices, neighbor lists, corner/edge flags, and an owner array. For win checking, I'll need to BFS the group containing the placed stone, check corner/edge coverage for fork/bridge conditions, and flood-fill the complement region to detect rings.

Estimating the cost of checking every empty cell for immediate wins across both players, I figure the full brute-force approach runs around 70ms, which should be acceptable, though I'm considering restricting the check to only cells connected to the new stone to speed things up further.

For the move evaluation itself, I'm planning to use 0-1 BFS distance transforms from each edge and corner to measure connectivity potential for each player, factoring in that stepping through own stones is free while opponent stones block the path entirely.

Doing full BFS for every candidate move would be too slow though — running 24 BFS passes across 169 possible moves adds up to over a second, which is too costly. So I need to either restrict which cells get fully evaluated (focusing on those near existing stones, or top candidates from a cheap heuristic) or find a way to reuse a single pre-move distance computation to score all moves at once, similar to resistance-based heuristics in Hex.

Placing at the junction cell of multiple paths should cut the combined distance sum more than placing elsewhere, though it's an approximation. Given the cost, it's probably more practical to just evaluate a limited pool of candidate moves (near existing stones or on good paths) with full evaluation rather than computing exact potential changes for every cell.

I should add a time-based cutoff to keep things safe, stopping candidate evaluation if it runs too long and returning the best found so far. Beyond simple edge-distance heuristics, what really matters is building connected groups toward edges/corners, blocking opponent threats, catching immediate wins/forced blocks, and detecting double-threat moves — plus checking after my move whether the opponent has an unstoppable winning reply.

Counting all my immediate winning moves after each candidate is too slow if done naively (roughly 5000 checks at 200µs each is a full second), so I need to restrict win-checking to cells adjacent to my existing groups to cut the cost down.

I'm estimating the cost of checking all these neighbor cells for threats — it could add up to hundreds of milliseconds, so I should trim candidates down to the top 8 or so by potential score instead, since a potential of 1 already signals a near-win threat.

I want to figure out whether counting cells with fork/bridge sum equal to 1 gives an accurate count of distinct winning moves, which requires being careful about whether the distance metric double-counts the placed cell itself.

So I'll define the distance excluding the cell itself, where a cell's cost to reach an edge is the minimum over neighbors of their cost plus their distance, and zero if the cell sits directly on that edge. With this, an empty cell whose three edge-distances sum to zero is an immediate fork/bridge win, and for an occupied cell that sum being zero just confirms an existing win. Ring-shaped threats aren't captured by this distance approach at all, so I'll need to handle those separately through exact win checks rather than folding them into the threat count.

For each candidate move, I'll place the stone and compute both my own and the opponent's distance maps across all twelve relevant directions, then derive a "closest to winning" score by taking the minimum combined fork/bridge distance over all reachable cells — acknowledging this is only an approximate measure since paths may overlap rather than being truly independent stones needed.

I also need to count immediate threats: if the opponent has one or more zero-distance winning cells after my move and I haven't blocked it, that candidate is effectively a loss. The final score should weigh the difference between opponent's proximity to winning and my own, factoring in that the opponent moves next and thus has a slight tempo advantage.

I could soften the metric using a sum over near-junction cells instead of a pure min, weighting closer distances more heavily so positions with equal min values still get differentiated by breadth of winning paths. I'm also weighing the computational cost of this extra scoring against the BFS calls already needed per candidate move.

Writing 0-1 BFS distance function...

I skip cells occupied by opponents since their distances never get used, using 0-1 BFS where zero-cost moves push to the front. For fork detection at a cell, I sort its distances to the six edges and sum the three smallest, being careful that corners are excluded from edge sources and treated as separate targets since they don't belong to any edge. Bridges linking corners still need separate handling, and candidate cells for forks are just empty cells with viable paths to three edges or corners.

To limit branching, I compute one-time distance maps for both players at the current position, then score each empty cell cheaply using its fork/bridge potential for me and for blocking the opponent, plus bonuses for adjacency to my stones and centrality, taking only the top-scoring candidates for deeper search.

For the opening move on an empty board, I'll default to playing the center. I also need to handle edge cases like converting numpy validity masks to plain booleans, and I should nail down exactly which adjacency scheme (axial offsets, hex neighbor rules) matches the actual board representation before relying on degree-count heuristics.

6. Offset rows, even rows shifted left instead.

For each candidate I need to compute the degree of every valid cell and check the histogram matches the expected pattern for a hex grid of this size — 6 corner cells with degree 3, edge cells with degree 4, and interior cells with degree 6. I'll pick whichever mapping produces that exact distribution, falling back to option 3 if none fit, then verify against the example cell (4,1).

Checking neighbor coordinates for (4,1) under option 3 against the known adjacency list, it matches up correctly. Now I want to verify that a 169-cell mask is actually consistent with a 15x15 grid by working out column cell counts and how odd columns are vertically offset relative to even columns.

Working through columns 5-8 confirms the offsets line up correctly, giving 14, 14, 13, and 13 cells respectively, and column 0 gives 8 cells — everything checks out. So this board layout is representable, with corners at (0,7), (14,7), (3,0), (10,0), (3,14), and (10,14).

For identifying edges, I need to find boundary cells where degree is less than 6 — corners have degree 3, edge cells have degree 4. I want to group edge cells into six connected components based on adjacency among degree-4 cells, each expected to have s-2 cells, then assign edge ids generically in case the component count isn't exactly 6.

I also want to implement an exact win check function that handles ring-based detection for immediate wins, and I'm thinking about caching the valid_mask computation globally since it's only available at call time.

I'm now writing out the core data structures — cell indices, neighbor lists, corner and edge lookups — followed by a BFS-based win check that traces connected same-owner groups and tracks which corners and edges they touch to determine if a ring win condition is satisfied.

Then I'm reasoning through the trickier win condition: detecting rings, which requires two things — checking if a boundary cell has all six neighbors held by the same player, and flooding from the board's outer edge through non-group cells to see if any get trapped inside, which would indicate a surrounding ring. I'm second-guessing whether the local six-neighbor check needs to be restricted to cells actually within the group.

I'm working through whether closing the ring necessarily means x sits adjacent to some interior cell, reasoning about cycle minimality in the hex grid — since removing x breaks the loop, x must be on the cycle, and I'm trying to confirm every cycle cell touches the enclosed interior for non-minimal loops too.

That's manageable performance-wise, and I can optimize further: since a winning shape always touches an own stone, I only need to check empty cells adjacent to my own stones as win candidates, and similarly restrict opponent threat checks to empty cells adjacent to opponent stones. Now I'm working out the per-candidate evaluation logic, starting with checking whether the opponent has an immediate win available after my move.

A cell counts if fork_sum or bridge_sum equals zero there, since that means the connecting structure is already complete via existing stones. I want to find the minimum stones needed to complete a threat, checking both empty cells and cells occupied by my own stones where junction distances sum through existing connections.

For scoring, I'll mirror this analysis for the opponent after their move, tallying their exact fork/bridge/ring threats, and if they have any immediate winning threat, the position score drops sharply.

If instead I have two or more distinct winning cells, that's near-certain victory since the opponent can only block one stone at a time — unless both threats happen to rely on the same cell, which I need to check since a fork/bridge win depends only on my own stones, not the opponent's placement.

Otherwise, I'm scoring based on the weighted difference between the opponent's best reply and my best move, plus tempo and softer positional terms. For tempo, I'm thinking about who keeps initiative: if I create exactly one threat, the opponent is forced to block and I move again, but if the opponent's reply creates a threat of their own, I have to consider whether I'm forced onto the defensive next.

I want a soft term rewarding having many cells near key junctions—summing decay values across the board and weighting them roughly against the tempo/threat difference, then tuning the scaling factors so the numbers stay in a sensible range.

For fork detection, summing shortest distances from a junction to three edges is a reasonable (if overestimated) proxy, since overlapping paths just mean the true cost is lower. This doesn't explicitly model blocking, but that's already captured through opp_best increasing when the opponent responds. A full 2-ply search evaluating my top candidates against the opponent's best replies would be more robust but is likely too costly given the board size, so I'll keep the heuristic simple for now.

I'm also considering opponent double-threat prevention — if my move lets them create two immediate wins at once, that's a loss condition requiring 2-ply lookahead, which I'll skip for now since it's partially handled elsewhere. Ring-based threats are already covered by the exact immediate-win checker for both attack and defense.

Writing BFS distance function...

Finishing the queue-based traversal logic... This standard 0-1 BFS variant handles zero-cost edges via front-insertion while ensuring distances converge correctly since sources start at distance zero at the edges. I'm thinking about how each full evaluation requires running twelve BFS passes for each player, and considering whether recomputing only the affected region near a placed cell could save time rather than redoing every pass from scratch.

Given the cost per candidate is roughly 12ms, I estimate the time budget allows evaluating around 30-45 candidates within a 0.6 second window, so I'm designing a cheap heuristic scoring function using the existing distance maps to pick which candidates deserve full evaluation — weighting how critical a cell is for my own path versus how much it would block the opponent, plus small bonuses for adjacency to either player's existing path.

For opening moves I'll default to a center bias when the board is empty, letting tiebreakers favor central cells since the heuristic scores are flat early on, and I'm considering whether to add a bonus for bridge-pattern extensions though it may already be covered by the junction measure. I'm also thinking through how the "my_best" evaluation behaves with just a single stone placed, using the minimum over junction cells.

On the defensive side, since scoring treats both players symmetrically, my move should naturally account for blocking too, though I only guard against immediate ring completions rather than more subtle double-threat setups, which simple bots rarely execute anyway. I'll track elapsed time with a performance counter and cut off candidate evaluation past roughly 0.65 seconds, and wrap the whole decision process in a try/except so any failure falls back to picking a random empty cell.

Corner cells sit outside the edge groupings but still count as passable spaces, and the bridge distance calculation treats each corner as its own source, summing the two smallest corner distances plus local cost at a junction cell. For forks, junction cells similarly sum distances to three edges — if my group already touches two edges at zero cost and the third is five steps away, the fork potential comes out to five.

I'm now setting up the code, building a helper that maps valid grid cells to indices and defines the axial neighbor offsets for the hex-like adjacency.

Defining more neighbor offset variants...

I'm figuring out a test to identify which coordinate system matches by comparing vertex degree distributions against expected counts of degree-3, degree-4, and degree-6 vertices for a hex-shaped grid of given side length, trying candidate systems in a fixed order with a fallback. I'm also thinking through whether boundary cells with degree 4 could reveal connected components.

I'm also making sure the code degrades gracefully if the shape isn't actually hexagonal—like a plain square grid where degree patterns won't match any candidate—by defaulting corner and edge labels to -1 and keeping distance and component bookkeeping safe from crashes regardless of how many components or edges are found.

Now I'm writing the evaluation function that BFS-searches distances from each edge and corner source to a target owner's stones, tracking the shortest completion distance and number of forks across cells not already claimed by the opponent.

For own stones, v==0 actually means the line is already won, which I need to handle separately. The sorting cost across 169 cells with two sorts plus arithmetic each should run around 0.7ms, which is acceptable — using Python's built-in sorted is fine for six elements rather than heapq. The bigger performance question is running 24 BFS passes per candidate; each BFS touches around 169 nodes with up to six neighbors, so roughly a thousand simple inner-loop operations, which should still be fast enough in Python.

That works out to about 0.4ms per BFS pass, so 24 passes plus eval sums brings each candidate to roughly 12ms, and with 30 candidates that's about 360ms total — I'll set an overall time budget of 0.7s and break early if I exceed it, capping candidates around 40 with a time guard. I'm considering whether I can halve the work by reusing state after a move, but I'll keep things simple for now rather than optimizing that. I'm writing the scoring function that updates ownership and computes threat counts for the move.

The 0.5 is small enough to keep, and I can drop the constant offset since it doesn't affect ranking. When facing multiple opponent threats, I should prioritize moves that actually block one of those winning cells, adding a bonus for that, and handle the cases where there's exactly one forced block versus multiple options to choose among.

For scoring each candidate empty cell, I'm computing my junction value and the opponent's junction value with a small penalty offset, then combining these with bonuses for adjacency to my own stones and the opponent's stones, plus a small penalty for distance from center.

I'm second-guessing whether raw junction value alone is a good proxy for move quality, since a cell near a corner with two zero edge-distances could rank artificially high without being tactically strong. I'm thinking about refining this by estimating how much placing a stone there actually improves my best path value, but algebraically that reduces to the same ranking as before, so I need a genuinely better heuristic, like weighting cells that lie on shortest paths.

Since a perfect proxy is complex, I'll instead broaden the candidate pool for diversity: combine the top cells ranked by my junction value, the top ones by opponent junction value, and cells adjacent to my existing stones, unioning them and capping the total around 36 given time constraints for full evaluation. I'm also weighing whether a cheaper incremental full-evaluation approach might let me consider more candidates within the ~12ms budget.

For edge cases, I want the fork sum to become infinite whenever there aren't enough edges, and bridge value to become infinite when connectivity is too low. Now I'm writing the exact win-check function, doing a BFS from the placed stone to track group membership and edge/corner masks.

Still writing win-check logic...

I realize the full flood is only needed for groups of size 6 or more, since a smaller group can't form a complete ring. I confirm the ring definition holds: a non-group cell that can't reach the boundary via 6-adjacency through other non-group cells is enclosed by the group, and boundary cells are simply those with degree less than 6.

For the eval design, I'm satisfied that summing junction distances still encourages reasonable spread-out play, similar to how human Havannah players naturally distribute stones toward different edges rather than clustering.

Now I'm writing the policy function structure with detection and board-building helpers, plus a fallback exception handler in case the main policy logic fails.

Defining neighbor-adjacency systems...

Still defining neighbor functions...

Now I'm working out how to validate whether a cell count corresponds to a proper hexagonal lattice arrangement, checking the degree distribution against expected counts of corner, edge, and interior vertices for a valid hex number.

For edges of the board, I'm identifying boundary non-corner cells, grouping them into connected components via BFS, and sorting for determinism so distance calculations from these edge sources are consistent. I'm also planning an evaluation function for board positions that precomputes power-of-two weights and finds the smallest few threat values efficiently without full sorting overhead.

For candidate move generation, I want evaluate_side to also return per-cell value arrays so I can score empty cells using a combination of my/opponent threat values, adjacency bonuses, and center distance penalties, then pick the top candidates by this cheap heuristic rather than exhaustively evaluating everything. I'm considering how mid-game ties in adjacency values might need tie-breaking since many empty cells near a large group could share the same value.

For the actual search loop, I'm evaluating candidates in cheap-score order with a time guard, breaking once time exceeds a threshold but guaranteeing at least one candidate gets evaluated even if time is already tight. I also need to handle immediate win/loss cases: return right away if I have a winning move, return the opponent's winning cell if they have exactly one, and if they have multiple winning cells, restrict my search to just those cells and pick the best among them since I can't prevent all of them anyway.

I'm double-checking that when opponent has no exact immediate winning cells in the normal path, the distance-based threat estimate should also come out to zero, keeping the two checks consistent, though I'll keep the exact check as a safeguard regardless. I'm also weighing how much danger an opponent's post-move threat count of 2 poses versus a fatal count of 1, which the exact check already handles.

Given time constraints, I'll skip deeper 2-ply lookahead refinement for top candidates and instead add lightweight tiebreak terms using board-center depth (via BFS distance from boundary) and adjacency measures. Now I'm writing out the full solution code.

Building the coordinate system and adjacency structure...

Grouping boundary cells into edges by finding connected components among non-corner boundary nodes...

Then I'm computing distances from the boundary via BFS to get depth values across the grid, and preparing to return a dictionary bundling corners, edges, and depth info. I'll cap edge counts defensively in case of unusual board shapes, then move on to writing the BFS helper as a closure for efficiency.

Reprocessing a node twice is harmless since it's using the current distance value at pop time. Now I'm writing the evaluation function that computes zero/blocked masks for each owner and runs BFS from each edge source to get distances.

Still writing distance calc...

Writing the scoring logic...

There's a caveat with mt==1: the opponent will just block my single threat, so the eval doesn't truly foresee it, but forcing moves that keep advancing still tend to help overall. Moving on, I'm setting up the policy function that caches the board structure by validity key so it only rebuilds when the valid-move mask changes.

I'm mapping ownership arrays for me and opponent, collecting empty cells, and defaulting to a center pick when the board is empty. Then I'm checking each empty cell for immediate winning moves by temporarily assigning ownership and running the win-check function.

Next I check for opponent immediate wins, and if there's exactly one blocking move needed I return it right away. Otherwise I move into evaluating both sides' positional strength (branch counts, threat counts, scores) to decide the best candidate move based on depth.

If opponent threats exist, I restrict candidates to those; otherwise I rank all empty cells with a heuristic combining threat minimization, adjacency to my pieces and opponent pieces, and depth, keeping the top 36. Then I loop through candidates within a time budget, scoring each and tracking the best move to return.

Given the timing math, I should tighten the safety margin—dropping the guard to 0.65s and capping candidates at 32 to stay comfortably under the limit, especially on slower hardware. I also want to verify that win-checking and group flood-fill operations stay cheap enough not to blow the budget.

For the soft-term weight, I'm weighing whether it might overshadow the discrete blocking metric—a move that reduces blocked count by one could score similarly to one that only boosts soft robustness by a few points. The soft term is meant to capture multiplicity of winning paths as a tiebreaker, but I need to make sure it doesn't dominate the more direct threat-blocking signal.

I also realize there's a defensive blind spot: our evaluation doesn't detect the opponent building toward a ring threat (needing five stones surrounding a cell). I'm thinking about adding a ring-awareness term that scans each cell's six neighbors for opponent stones—five filled with the sixth empty means an immediate threat, while four filled with two empty signals a ring-in-two that should be penalized.

This calculation is cheap enough to run every evaluation, so I'll fold in modest weights, rewarding my own ring potential lightly while weighting the opponent's ring potential more heavily as a defensive priority.

I also want to verify the fork definition against edges — corners aren't counted as part of an edge, which matches what I already have — and confirm bridges connect corner-to-corner correctly, being blocked only if the opponent occupies that corner cell.

Writing the win-check flood fill...

Finishing the flood-fill check: if not all cells are marked seen, that means some non-group cell remains unreached, confirming a ring exists. I'm also verifying the size and boundary logic hold for both ring types, then considering what fallback to use if the group data lacks certain fields.

As a final safety net, I want to double-check that the returned move is actually legal and unoccupied, falling back to any valid empty cell otherwise. Estimating runtime: each BFS pass costs roughly 0.35ms, and with 12 BFS calls per side across 32 candidate moves, total evaluation time lands around 320ms, which seems acceptable.

I'm handling the case where opponent has multiple winning threats by evaluating each of those candidate cells and picking the best. I also want to confirm numpy indexing works fine for the valid_mask checks, and I'm planning to special-case the very first move by simply returning the board's center.

I'm now writing a helper function that scans interior cells and measures each one's ring potential, counting how many neighbors belong to each owner to detect near-encirclement patterns.

Then I'm finalizing the scoring formula, blending together material balance, mobility, threat bonus, ring bonus/penalty, depth, and adjacency into a single weighted heuristic value for the position.
